title: Why Do We Dream? What Science Actually Knows
script:
Hey everyone, welcome back to the channel.
If you're new here, we make videos about science, psychology and how the brain works, every single week.
So make sure you hit subscribe and turn on notifications so you never miss one.
Before we start, a quick thank you to everyone who commented on the last video, there were so many great questions.
A lot of you asked about sleep, and honestly that's what got me thinking about today's topic.
I've actually been sleeping really badly this month, which is a bit ironic for someone making a video about sleep.
I moved apartments, the new place is noisy, and my neighbour has a dog that barks at exactly six in the morning.
Anyway, let's get into it.
So, dreams.
Every night you spend roughly two hours dreaming, whether you remember it or not.
Most vivid dreams happen during REM sleep, which stands for rapid eye movement sleep.
During REM, your brain is almost as active as when you're awake, but your body is mostly paralysed so you don't act out your dreams.
You go through several sleep cycles a night, and the REM periods get longer towards the morning.
That's why the dreams you remember are usually the ones just before you wake up.
So why do we dream at all? Scientists don't have one single answer, but there are a few strong ideas.
The first idea is memory.
During sleep, the brain replays and sorts the day's experiences, deciding what to keep and what to let go.
In experiments, people who learned a task and then slept performed better than people who stayed awake.
Some researchers think dreams are a side effect of this sorting process, like seeing the files while they're being organised.
The second idea is emotional processing.
REM sleep seems to help take the sting out of difficult experiences.
Dreams might be a safe place to replay emotional events with less of the stress attached.
The third idea is threat simulation.
This theory says dreams let us rehearse dangerous situations, like being chased, so we're better prepared in real life.
It would explain why so many dreams are about being chased, falling or being late.
And the fourth idea, which is older, is the activation-synthesis hypothesis.
It says the brainstem sends out fairly random signals during REM, and the rest of the brain tries to make a story out of them.
So the dream is the brain's best attempt to make sense of noise.
Now let me quickly recap the first idea again, because it's important.
During sleep, the brain replays the day's experiences and decides what to keep.
People who slept after learning something remembered it better than people who stayed awake.
So dreams might be connected to that memory sorting.
Okay, so that's basically the main theories, I hope you found this useful.
But wait, there's one more thing a lot of people ask about, which is lucid dreaming.
A lucid dream is when you realise you're dreaming while you're still in the dream.
Some people can even steer what happens next.
Studies have shown that lucid dreamers can signal to researchers with specific eye movements while they are asleep.
That's how scientists confirmed lucid dreaming is real and not just a story people tell afterwards.
You can make lucid dreams more likely by keeping a dream journal and checking during the day whether you're dreaming.
So which theory is right?
The honest answer is that it's probably not just one.
Dreams likely help with memory and with emotions, and some of the strange details may simply be the brain filling gaps.
What researchers agree on is that sleep itself, especially REM sleep, matters a lot for how you think and feel the next day.
So if you want better dreams, the boring advice is the real advice: sleep enough, at regular times, in a dark quiet room.
Which, in my case, means finding a way to deal with that dog.
Let me know in the comments what the strangest dream you've ever had was.
Thanks for watching, and I'll see you in the next one.
